**Miguel Angel Cardona** (born July 11, 1975) is an American educator who served as the 12th [United States Secretary of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") under [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") from March 2, 2021 to January 20, 2025. A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), he was confirmed by the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") by a vote of 64–33 on March 1, 2021.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-1) Cardona previously served as commissioner of the [Connecticut State Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_State_Department_of_Education "Connecticut State Department of Education") from 2019 to 2021.

A native of [Meriden, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriden,_Connecticut "Meriden, Connecticut"), Cardona began his career as a fourth-grade teacher at Israel Putnam Elementary School in Meriden. In 2003, at the age of twenty-seven, he was named principal of Meriden's Hanover School, making him the youngest principal in the state.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-3)

## Early life and education

Miguel Cardona was born on July 11, 1975, in [Meriden, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriden,_Connecticut "Meriden, Connecticut"), to [Puerto Rican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rican_people "Puerto Rican people") parents.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:2-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-5) Cardona grew up speaking Spanish as his [first language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_language "First language") and started to learn English when entering [kindergarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindergarten "Kindergarten").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:0-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-7) His father is a retired police officer in Meriden.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:3-8) Cardona was raised in a [housing project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_project "Housing project") in Meriden and graduated from the [H.C. Wilcox Technical High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.C._Wilcox_Technical_High_School "H.C. Wilcox Technical High School"), where he was a part of the automotive studies program. He visits his Alma Mater frequently, recently being the guest speaker for the class of 2023.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-csde-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-ctmirror.org-11)

Cardona earned a Bachelor of Science in education from [Central Connecticut State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Connecticut_State_University "Central Connecticut State University") in New Britain, CT in 1997. He obtained a Master of Science in bilingual and bicultural education at [University of Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Connecticut "University of Connecticut") (UConn) in 2001. In 2004, he completed a professional [sixth year certification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_specialist "Educational specialist") at UConn where he earned a [doctor of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Education "Doctor of Education") in 2011.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-csde-10)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:1-12)

Cardona's dissertation, titled *Sharpening the Focus of Political Will to Address Achievement Disparities*, studied the gaps between [English-language learners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English-language_learner "English-language learner") and their classmates.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:1-12)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:0-6) His doctoral major advisor was Barry G. Sheckley and his associate advisor was Casey D. Cobb.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:1-12)

## Career

Cardona began his career as a fourth-grade teacher at Israel Putnam Elementary School in [Meriden, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meriden,_Connecticut "Meriden, Connecticut"). In 2003, at Hanover Elementary School, he was promoted and made the youngest [principal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_teacher "Head teacher") in the state's history for ten years. From 2015 to 2019, Cardona served as assistant superintendent for teaching and learning in his home town.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-14)

Cardona was also an adjunct professor of education in the University of Connecticut's Department of Educational Leadership.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-15) During his career, he has focused on closing gaps between English-language learners and their peers.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:0-6)

In August 2019, Governor [Ned Lamont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Lamont "Ned Lamont") appointed Cardona as [commissioner of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut_State_Department_of_Education "Connecticut State Department of Education"); Cardona was the first Latino to hold the position.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-csde-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-ctmirror.org-11) During his tenure, Cardona helped oversee state schools' response to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Connecticut "COVID-19 pandemic in Connecticut"), where he expressed concerns over the long-term mental health impacts of [remote education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remote_education "Remote education") on students.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-:3-8)

## Secretary of Education (2021–2025)

### Nomination and confirmation

In December 2020, Cardona emerged as a candidate for [United States secretary of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") in [Joe Biden's cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Joe_Biden "Cabinet of Joe Biden"). Biden began to lean toward Cardona over two other "high-profile" teachers' union leaders, [Lily Eskelsen García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lily_Eskelsen_García "Lily Eskelsen García") and [Randi Weingarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randi_Weingarten "Randi Weingarten"). By choosing Cardona over the two, Biden "appeared to have sidestepped any sibling rivalry between the [NEA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Education_Association "National Education Association") and [AFT.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Federation_of_Teachers "American Federation of Teachers")"[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-17)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/P20210805CS-0453_%2851478523057%29.jpg/250px-P20210805CS-0453_%2851478523057%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:P20210805CS-0453_(51478523057).jpg)Cardona talks with reporters during a press briefing on August 5, 2021, at the White House.

Cardona was brought to the attention of Biden by [Linda Darling-Hammond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Darling-Hammond "Linda Darling-Hammond"), the leader of the transition's education secretary search efforts, a role she also filled for [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") in 2008. Darling-Hammond and Cardona had worked together on numerous projects.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-ctmirror.org-11) *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* noted that "[Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic "Hispanic") lawmakers are stressing in particular the need for a Latina to join the administration."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-18)

Cardona appeared before the [Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Health,_Education,_Labor_and_Pensions "United States Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions") on February 3, 2021.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-19) On February 25, his nomination was advanced by the Senate on a [cloture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloture "Cloture") vote of 66–32.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-20) Cardona was confirmed on March 1, 2021, by a 64–33 vote. Cardona took his oath of office on March 1, 2021, and was ceremonially sworn in by Vice President [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris") on March 2, 2021.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-21)

### Tenure

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/The_Atlantic_Interview_with_Miguel_Cardona_on_14_December_2023_-_2.jpg/250px-The_Atlantic_Interview_with_Miguel_Cardona_on_14_December_2023_-_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Atlantic_Interview_with_Miguel_Cardona_on_14_December_2023_-_2.jpg)Cardona speaks on a panel hosted by *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")* in December 2023.

Throughout his tenure as Secretary of Education, Cardona was responsible for implementing several forms of forgiveness for [student loans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_loans_in_the_United_States "Student loans in the United States").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-auto-22) The administration's most sweeping attempt to do so, which would have forgiven about $430 billion in student loan principles, was struck down by the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") on June 30, 2023, in *[Biden v. Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_v._Nebraska "Biden v. Nebraska")*.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-23) Following the *Biden v. Nebraska* decision, Cardona announced a series of smaller and more targeted student loan forgiveness programs, and the Department of Education has reemphasized the [Public Service Loan Forgiveness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Service_Loan_Forgiveness "Public Service Loan Forgiveness") program to reduce the student debt of people working full-time in [public service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_service "Public service").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-auto-22)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-25) In December 2023, Cardona announced that the administration had forgiven about $132 billion of student debt in its first three years.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-auto-22) At President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")’s [2024 State of The Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_State_of_the_Union_Address "2024 State of the Union Address"), Cardona was the [designated survivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Designated_survivor "Designated survivor").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-26)

In December 2023, simplified [Free Application for Federal Student Aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Application_for_Federal_Student_Aid "Free Application for Federal Student Aid") (FAFSA) forms were released after a two-month delay.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-27) By late March 2024, there was a backlog of 6 million applications.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-28) On April 26, the Education Department announced that the top official in charge of federal financial student aid would step down.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-29) Colleges across the country were obliged to delay their decision deadlines as students were still waiting for financial aid offers. On April 30, Cardona was questioned at a congressional hearing about the troubled introduction of the new form.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-30) On May 7, Cardona apologized at another congressional hearing.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-31)

## Personal life

In 2002, Cardona married Marissa Pérez, a [family-school liaison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_social_worker "School social worker").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-Alverio-32) Pérez was named [Miss Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Connecticut "Miss Connecticut") in 2001 and [Miss Connecticut Teen USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Connecticut_Teen_USA "Miss Connecticut Teen USA") in 1996.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-33)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-Alverio-32) Cardona and his wife have two children: a son, Miguel Jr., and a daughter, Celine.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-csde-10) Cardona is [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona#cite_note-34)

# U.S. Department of Education

Election Day is almost here. Millions of voters rely on Ballotpedia. Help us inform them with a [gift today](https://donate.ballotpedia.org/campaign/856148/donate).

From Ballotpedia

Jump to: [navigation](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#mw-navigation), [search](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#p-search)

See also: *[United States education agencies](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_education_agencies "United States education agencies")*

The **U.S. Department of Education** is a United States executive department established in 1980. The department was formed to promote educational excellence and ensure equal opportunity for public schooling.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1) Of the 15 Cabinet agencies, the U.S. Department of Education has the smallest staff and the third largest discretionary budget.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-2)  

[Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") is the U.S. secretary of education. [Click here](https://ballotpedia.org/Confirmation_process_for_Donald_Trump%27s_Cabinet_nominees,_2025-2026 "Confirmation process for Donald Trump's Cabinet nominees, 2025-2026") to learn more about her confirmation process.

## History

Education in the U.S. is primarily the responsibility of states and local districts. The [United States Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") does not mention any role for the federal government in education, and, according to the [Tenth Amendment](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution"), anything not mentioned in the [Constitution](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Constitution "United States Constitution") is left to the states to decide. A federal department of education was originally created in 1867 to help the states set up school systems by gathering information about teaching, schools, and teachers. The current U.S. Department of Education was established by [Congress](https://ballotpedia.org/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") in 1980. It united several existing offices across different agencies into a Cabinet level agency located in the executive branch. Over the years, the location of the department in the government and its name has changed several times, and its scope, number of personnel and budget has significantly increased.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[3]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-3)

The department's mission of fostering educational excellence and equal access arose out of the cultural and political events in the post-World War II era. The [National Defense Education Act (NDEA)](https://ballotpedia.org/National_Defense_Education_Act_(NDEA) "National Defense Education Act (NDEA)"), the first comprehensive federal education law, was passed by Congress in 1958 in response to the Soviet launch of Sputnik during the Cold War. The department added its "public access" mission in response to anti-poverty and civil rights legislation of the 1960s and 1970s.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[4]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-4)

Although the federal government provides only about 12 percent of the overall education spending of $1.15 trillion, the role of the federal government in setting education policy has grown considerably over the last several decades. The department implements laws passed by Congress and administers grants to states for certain programs, such as the [No Child Left Behind Act](https://ballotpedia.org/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act"), [Race to the Top](https://ballotpedia.org/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") and Title One School Improvement Grants.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-DOEabout-1)[[5]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-6)

### Timeline

The following is a list of important dates in the history of the federal government's role in education:[[7]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-hist-7)[[8]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-8)

- 1862: The First Morrill Act provided the first federal aid for higher education by donating land for setting up colleges.[[9]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-9)
- 1890: The Second Morrill Act established a support system for land-grant colleges and universities.
- 1896: The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case *[Plessy v. Ferguson](https://ballotpedia.org/Plessy_v._Ferguson "Plessy v. Ferguson")* legalized segregation in "separate but equal" schools.
- 1917: The Smith-Hughes Act extended federal aid to vocational education programs.
- 1944: The GI Bill authorized assistance to veterans for postsecondary schools.
- 1946: The Georgia-Barden Act established agricultural, industrial and home economics classes.
- 1954: The U.S. Supreme Court case *[Brown v. Board of Education](https://ballotpedia.org/Brown_v._Board_of_Education "Brown v. Board of Education")* outlawed segregation precedent set in *Plessy v. Ferguson*.
- 1958: The [National Defense Education Act (NDEA)](https://ballotpedia.org/National_Defense_Education_Act_(NDEA) "National Defense Education Act (NDEA)") supported loans for college students; improved science, technology and foreign language support in elementary and secondary schools; and provided fellowships in response to the Cold War.
- 1964: Title VI of the [Civil Rights Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1964 "Civil Rights Act of 1964") prohibited discrimination based on race, color or national origin in public schools.
- 1965: Title I of the [Elementary and Secondary Education Act](https://ballotpedia.org/Elementary_and_Secondary_Education_Act_of_1965 "Elementary and Secondary Education Act of 1965") gave federal aid to schools in poor rural and urban areas.
- 1965: The Higher Education Act authorized federal aid for poor postsecondary students.
- 1970: Standardized tests were given to public schools and the results were reported to the government and public in an effort to hold educators accountable.
- 1972: Title IX of the Education Amendments prohibited discrimination based on sex in public schools.
- 1973: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act prohibited discrimination based on disability in public schools.
- 1980: Congress passed the "Department of Education Organization Act," (Public Law 96-88 of October 1979).
- 2001: The [No Child Left Behind Act](https://ballotpedia.org/No_Child_Left_Behind_Act "No Child Left Behind Act") (NCLB) increased education funding and established standards-based testing reforms.
- 2010: The [Race to the Top](https://ballotpedia.org/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") program encouraged states to compete for federal grants in education.
- 2025: Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the U.S. Department of Education would transfer the administration of some federal K-12 and higher education programs to the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Labor "U.S. Department of Labor"), the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Interior "U.S. Department of the Interior"), the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services"), and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State").[[10]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-10)

## [Noteworthy events](https://ballotpedia.org/Noteworthy_events "Noteworthy events")

#### U.S. Department of Education enters into agreement to transfer student loan portfolio to the Treasury Department (2026)

On March 19, 2026, Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the Department of Education would transfer its portfolio of student loans to the [U.S. Department of the Treasury](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Treasury "U.S. Department of the Treasury"). These loans were worth about $1.7 trillion in total, as of March 2026.[[13]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-13)

#### U.S. Department of Education enters into two more agreements to transfer administration of some education programs to two federal agencies (2026)

On February 23, 2026, Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services") and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State") would administer additional federal K-12 and higher education programs through two further interagency agreements. McMahon said the State Department would assist in managing foreign gift and contract reporting for certain domestic public and private institutions of higher education (IHEs) as required by Section 117 of the Higher Education Act of 1965. McMahon said the Health and Human Services Department would assist in administering the following:[[14]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-14)

- the School Emergency Response to Violence (Project SERV)
- School Safety National Activities, Ready to Learn Programming
- Full-Service Community Schools
- Promise Neighborhoods
- Statewide Family Engagement Centers

#### U.S. Department of Education enters into agreements to transfer administration of some education programs to four federal agencies (2025)

On November 18, Education Secretary [Linda McMahon](https://ballotpedia.org/Linda_McMahon "Linda McMahon") announced the [U.S. Department of Labor](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Labor "U.S. Department of Labor"), the [U.S. Department of the Interior](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_the_Interior "U.S. Department of the Interior"), the [U.S. Department of Health and Human Services](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services "U.S. Department of Health and Human Services"), and the [U.S. Department of State](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_State "U.S. Department of State") would administer some federal K-12 and higher education programs through six interagency agreements with the U.S. Department of Education.[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-15)[[16]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-16)

McMahon said the partnerships supported President [Donald Trump's](https://ballotpedia.org/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") March 20, 2025, [executive order](https://ballotpedia.org/Executive_Order:_Improving_Education_Outcomes_by_Empowering_Parents,_States,_and_Communities_(Donald_Trump,_2025) "Executive Order: Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities (Donald Trump, 2025)") that called for closing the Education Department and returning its functions to the states.[[17]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-17) McMahon said, "The Trump Administration is taking bold action to break up the federal education bureaucracy and return education to the states. Cutting through layers of red tape in Washington is one essential piece of our final mission."[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-15)

McMahon announced the following partnerships:[[15]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-press-15)

- **U.S. Department of Labor**: Elementary and Secondary Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Labor**: Postsecondary Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of the Interior**: Indian Education Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**: Foreign Medical Accreditation Partnership
- **U.S. Department of Health and Human Services**: Child Care Access Means Parents in School Partnership
- **U.S. Department of State**: International Education and Foreign Language Studies Partnership

#### Supreme Court allows President Trump's order to dismantle DOE to continue pending litigation (2025)

The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") allowed the Trump administration to resume enforcement of a March 20 executive order to shut down the Department of Education (DOE), pending the administration's appeal of a May 22, 2025, ruling by U.S. District Judge [Myong Joun](https://ballotpedia.org/Myong_Joun "Myong Joun") that blocked it. The May ruling also ordered the administration to reinstate fired workers. In a lawsuit, several education groups claimed that the Trump executive order hindered the department's ability to fulfill its mandated responsibilities, which include providing financial aid, supporting special education, and protecting civil rights. The executive order, titled "Improving Education Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities," was written to shift education authority to the states and close the DOE beyond its "core necessities" of distributing Title I funding for low-income schools, money for special education, and Pell grants. On March 11, 2025, the Trump Administration laid off 1,300 workers, leaving the department with half its former workforce and most significantly impacting Federal Student Aid, the Office for Civil Rights, and the [Institute of Education Sciences](https://ballotpedia.org/Institute_of_Education_Sciences "Institute of Education Sciences"). Joun wrote that the layoffs "will likely cripple the Department," and noted that "the Department cannot be shut down without Congress’s approval." The Trump administration filed an appeal days later. The [U.S. Supreme Court](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Supreme_Court "U.S. Supreme Court") allowed the Trump administrative to resume enforcement of the executive order, pending the appeal.[[18]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-20)

#### Trump administration rescinds Obama-era guidance document (2018)

*See also: [Guidance (administrative state)](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance_(administrative_state) "Guidance (administrative state)") and [Rulemaking](https://ballotpedia.org/Rulemaking "Rulemaking")*

The Trump administration rescinded [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents in July 2018 that had been issued by the DOE under the Obama administration. The [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents encouraged institutions of higher education to consider race as a factor in the admissions process as a means to achieving student diversity. The documents provided legal recommendations and contextual examples for schools considering race as a component of the admissions process.[[21]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-21)[[22]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-wsj-22)

The decision to rescind the DOE's [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents occurred in light of an investigation launched by the [U.S. Department of Justice](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Justice "U.S. Department of Justice") (DOJ) in the summer of 2017 regarding allegations that Harvard University discriminated against Asian-American applicants by holding them to a higher standard than other applicants.[[22]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-wsj-22)[[23]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-23)

Attorney General [Jeff Sessions](https://ballotpedia.org/Jeff_Sessions "Jeff Sessions") announced the policy change on July 3, 2018. In his announcement, Sessions stated that the DOE is required to adopt new regulations through the [rulemaking](https://ballotpedia.org/Rulemaking "Rulemaking") process, which provides members of the public with the opportunity to offer feedback on [proposed rules](https://ballotpedia.org/Proposed_rule "Proposed rule") during [public comment periods](https://ballotpedia.org/Comment_period "Comment period"). He discouraged the agency from implementing regulations through [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents, which are issued by agencies in order to explain, interpret, or advise interested parties about rules, laws, and procedures:[[21]](https://ballotpedia.org/U.S._Department_of_Education#cite_note-cnn-21)

Sessions previously instructed the DOJ to refrain from issuing regulations through [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance") documents in a November 2017 agency memo. For more information about Sessions' DOJ memo on [guidance](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance "Guidance"), [**click here**](https://ballotpedia.org/Guidance_(administrative_state)#Presidential_administrations_on_guidance "Guidance (administrative state)").

**Mitchell McGeever** "**Mick**" **Zais** (born December 10, 1946) is an American education official and former general who served as the acting [United States secretary of education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-1) He previously served as the 17th [South Carolina Superintendent of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_Superintendent_of_Education "South Carolina Superintendent of Education") from 2011 to 2015. Before winning the election as superintendent, he served as President of [Newberry College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newberry_College "Newberry College") for ten years.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-2) Prior to that he reached the rank of Brigadier General in the United States Army.

On January 7, 2021, Education Secretary [Betsy DeVos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos "Betsy DeVos") submitted her resignation to the [President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") because of the [2021 storming of the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_storming_of_the_United_States_Capitol "2021 storming of the United States Capitol").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-3) As deputy secretary, Zais succeeded DeVos as [acting secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Vacancies_Reform_Act_of_1998 "Federal Vacancies Reform Act of 1998").

## Early life and education

Zais was born in [Fort Bragg, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Bragg,_North_Carolina "Fort Bragg, North Carolina").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-4) He earned a Bachelor of Science degree in engineering from [West Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point "West Point"), a Master of Science and a doctorate in social psychology and organizational behavior both from the [University of Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Washington "University of Washington") and a Master of Arts in military history from the [School of Advanced Military Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_of_Advanced_Military_Studies "School of Advanced Military Studies") at the [United States Army Command and General Staff College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Command_and_General_Staff_College "United States Army Command and General Staff College").

## Career

### Military

During his military career, Zais served in a wide variety of infantry units in [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam "Vietnam"), the United States, and [Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea"). He commanded two rifle companies, an infantry battalion, a light infantry brigade, and served as deputy commanding general at [Fort Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Riley "Fort Riley"), [Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas "Kansas"). Zais was also the Pentagon's Chief of War Plans. As an assistant professor at West Point for three years, he taught organizational behavior, leadership, and management consulting.

Zais served as a White House aide and in Panama as executive assistant to the four-star commander of all U.S. forces in Central and South America. In Kuwait, he was commanding general of U.S. and Allied forces. He also served as commanding general of Operation Provide Refuge, the task force that cared for 4,000 Kosovo refugees who entered the United States. Zais's last military assignment was as Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army Reserve Command, the headquarters that administers the 184,000 part-time Reservists, 9,000 civilian employees, and 11,000 full-time military members of the Army Reserve. At the time of his retirement from the military Zais held the rank of Brigadier General.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-5)

Zais's military awards and decorations include the Distinguished Service Medal; the Defense Superior Service Medal; the Legion of Merit; the Bronze Star; the Meritorious Service Medal; the Air Medal; the Republic of Vietnam Campaign Medal; the Humanitarian Service Medal; the Ranger, Airborne, and Combat Infantryman's Badges; and the South Carolina Meritorious Service Medal.

### Newberry College

Zais became the president of [Newberry College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newberry_College "Newberry College") in August 2000. During his time at Newberry, both enrollment and endowment nearly doubled. During the last three years of his tenure, Newberry College was named by U.S. News & World Report as one of America's best colleges.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-6) He retired in June 2010, just prior to running for state Superintendent of Education.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-7)

### South Carolina Superintendent of Education

#### 2010 election

See also: [South Carolina elections, 2010 § Superintendent of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_elections,_2010#Superintendent_of_Education "South Carolina elections, 2010")

Zais ran in a crowded field for the [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") nomination. Zais was the top vote getter in the primary but did not clear the necessary 50% threshold. Zais defeated Elizabeth Moffly in the run-off. He faced [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") [Frank Holleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Holleman "Frank Holleman"), [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian "Libertarian") Tim Moultrie and two minor party candidates in the November general election. Zais won with 51% of the vote.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-9)

#### Tenure and retirement

Zais opposed implementation of the [Common Core State Standards Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Core_State_Standards_Initiative "Common Core State Standards Initiative") in South Carolina and withdrew from the state's participation in the federal [Race to the Top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top "Race to the Top") grant competition. Zais supported the state's Governor to have the power to appoint the State Superintendent of Education, a position shared by a former Democratic Superintendent as well as his successor in the position.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-11) By the end of Zais's tenure, South Carolina's on-time high school graduation rates hit an all-time high of over 80% of students finishing within four-years.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-12) Zais decided not to run for re-election and endorsed [Sally Atwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina_elections,_2014#Superintendent_of_Education "South Carolina elections, 2014"), widow of [Lee Atwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Atwater "Lee Atwater"), as his replacement. In the 2014 election, Republican educator and former legislator, [Molly Mitchell Spearman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Mitchell_Spearman "Molly Mitchell Spearman"), won by a wide margin and replaced Zais as South Carolina's State Superintendent of Education.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-13)

### U.S. Department of Education

On October 5, 2017, [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") announced his intention to nominate Zais to serve as the [United States Deputy Secretary of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Deputy_Secretary_of_Education "United States Deputy Secretary of Education").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-14) He was confirmed by the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") by a vote of 50–48 on May 16, 2018.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-15)

After [Betsy DeVos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos "Betsy DeVos") resigned as Secretary of Education on January 7, 2021, after the [storming of the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_storming_of_the_United_States_Capitol "2021 storming of the United States Capitol"), Zais assumed the office of secretary on January 8. He remained in the position until January 20, 2021, when President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden") nominated [Phil Rosenfelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt "Phil Rosenfelt"), the former Acting General Counsel of the United States Department of Education, to serve in an acting capacity as Secretary of Education until [Miguel Cardona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona "Miguel Cardona"), the President's nominee, was confirmed by the Senate.

In June 2023, Zais endorsed [Tim Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Scott "Tim Scott") in the [2024 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-16)In September 2025, Zais was named the government relations chair for the Boston 2026 World Expo.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-17)

## Personal life

Zais has a daughter, Ashley, who was Miss South Carolina USA in 2007.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-18) His father, [Melvin Zais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_Zais "Melvin Zais"), was a four-star general in the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-19)

He served as president of the [American Philatelic Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Philatelic_Society "American Philatelic Society") a non-profit organization focused on [philately](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philately "Philately") or [stamp collecting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stamp_collecting "Stamp collecting"), from August 2016 until his appointment as deputy secretary of education in May 2018.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Zais#cite_note-20) At the time he noted that with his role at the Department of Education he would "have to resign from all boards and all other employment."

**Philip H. Rosenfelt** is an American lawyer and civil servant who served as the acting [United States Secretary of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") from January 20, 2021 to March 2, 2021. He served in this same position under the [Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "First presidency of Donald Trump") prior to the Senate confirming [Betsy DeVos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betsy_DeVos "Betsy DeVos").

On November 23, 2016, President-elect [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") announced Betsy DeVos to be his designee for Secretary of Education.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt#cite_note-Buzzfeed_161123-1) Prior to DeVos' confirmation by the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"), Rosenfelt was the acting Secretary of Education. Rosenfelt served from January 20, 2017 to February 7, 2017, when DeVos was sworn in.

With the departure of Betsy DeVos at the end of former president Donald Trump's term, Rosenfelt once again assumed the position of acting secretary; this time under the administration of President [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"). Rosenfelt was serving in an acting capacity under Joe Biden's administration until the Senate reviewed the nomination of [Miguel Cardona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona "Miguel Cardona") for the position.

## Personal life

Born in Paterson, New Jersey, Rosenfelt is of [Jewish descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_descent "Jewish descent"). He received a bachelor of science degree from the [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), his juris doctor from [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), and his [LLM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Laws "Master of Laws") from [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University"). He began his service in the federal government in 1971 at the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt#cite_note-2)

## Career

In 2005, Rosenfelt assumed the position of Deputy General Counsel of the United States Department of Education for Program Service. He served under the administration of [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"). He has continued to serve in that capacity since his appointment.

From January 20, 2017 to April 23, 2018, Rosenfelt served as the acting [General Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Counsel "General Counsel") of the [United States Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Education "United States Department of Education").

He has been designated as the acting [United States Secretary of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Education "United States Secretary of Education") on two occasions; the first of these from January 20, 2017 to February 7, 2017, and the second from January 20, 2021 until March 2, 2021. He has been replaced by [President Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_Biden "President Biden")'s nominee [Miguel Cardona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_Cardona "Miguel Cardona") as he was confirmed by the Senate.

Currently, Rosenfelt serves as the Deputy General Counsel for Program Service in the Office of the General Counsel at the Department of Education.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Rosenfelt#cite_note-3)

**Brazilian clubs that qualified for the 2025 Copa Libertadores**

According to CONMEBOL’s official tournament details and recent coverage, Brazil earned **seven** spots in the 2025 edition. The qualifying path produced the following Brazilian teams:

| Club | Qualification route |
|------|---------------------|

International football competition

The **2025 Copa CONMEBOL Libertadores** was the 66th edition of the [CONMEBOL Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copa_Libertadores "Copa Libertadores") (also referred to as the *Copa Libertadores*), [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America")'s premier club [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") tournament organized by [CONMEBOL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONMEBOL "CONMEBOL"). The competition began on 4 February and ended on 29 November 2025,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-1) with [the final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores_final "2025 Copa Libertadores final") played at [Estadio Monumental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estadio_Monumental_"U" "Estadio Monumental "U"") in [Lima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lima "Lima"), Peru.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-3)

Brazilian club [Flamengo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_Flamengo "CR Flamengo") won their fourth Copa Libertadores title, defeating fellow Brazilian side [Palmeiras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SE_Palmeiras "SE Palmeiras") 1–0 in the final.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-4) As winners of the 2025 Copa Libertadores, Flamengo earned the right to play against the winners of the [2025 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Sudamericana "2025 Copa Sudamericana") in the [2026 Recopa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Recopa_Sudamericana "2026 Recopa Sudamericana"). They also automatically qualified for the [2025 FIFA Intercontinental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_FIFA_Intercontinental_Cup "2025 FIFA Intercontinental Cup"), the [2029 FIFA Club World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2029_FIFA_Club_World_Cup "2029 FIFA Club World Cup") and the [2026 Copa Libertadores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Copa_Libertadores "2026 Copa Libertadores") group stage.

[Botafogo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botafogo_de_Futebol_e_Regatas "Botafogo de Futebol e Regatas") were the defending champions, but were eliminated by [LDU Quito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L.D.U._Quito "L.D.U. Quito") in the round of 16.

With Flamengo's triumph, Brazil tied Argentina as the nation with the most Copa Libertadores championships with 25 titles. This was as well the seventh consecutive edition won by Brazilian clubs.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-5)

## Teams

The following 47 teams from the 10 CONMEBOL member associations qualified for the tournament:

- Copa Libertadores champions
- Copa Sudamericana champions
- Brazil: 7 berths
- Argentina: 6 berths
- All other associations: 4 berths each

The entry stage was determined as follows:[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-6)

- Group stage: 28 teams
  - Copa Libertadores champions
  - Copa Sudamericana champions
  - Teams which qualified for berths 1–5 from Argentina and Brazil
  - Teams which qualified for berths 1–2 from all other associations
- Second stage: 13 teams
  - Teams which qualified for berths 6–7 from Brazil
  - Team which qualified for berth 6 from Argentina
  - Teams which qualified for berths 3–4 from Chile and Colombia
  - Teams which qualified for berth 3 from all other associations
- First stage: 6 teams
  - Teams which qualified for berth 4 from Bolivia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay and Venezuela

The draw for the qualifying stages was held on 19 December 2024, 12:00 [PYT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_in_Paraguay "Time in Paraguay") ([UTC−3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC−03:00 "UTC−03:00")), at the CONMEBOL Convention Centre in [Luque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luque "Luque"), [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-22)

Teams were seeded by their *CONMEBOL Clubs ranking* as of 16 December 2024 (shown in parentheses),[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-ranking-23) taking into account the following three factors:[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-24)

1. Performance in the last 10 years, taking into account Copa Libertadores and Copa Sudamericana results in the period 2015–2024.
2. Historical coefficient, taking into account Copa Libertadores and Copa Sudamericana results in the period 1960–2014 and 2002–2014 respectively.
3. Local tournament champion, with bonus points awarded to domestic league champions of the last 10 years.

For the first stage, the six teams were drawn into three ties (E1–E3), with the teams from Pot 1 hosting the second leg.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-draw_procedure-18)

## Qualifying stages

Main article: [2025 Copa Libertadores qualifying stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores_qualifying_stages "2025 Copa Libertadores qualifying stages")

In the qualifying stages, each tie was played on a home-and-away [two-legged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-legged_tie "Two-legged tie") basis. If tied on aggregate, [extra time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtime_(sports)#Association_football "Overtime (sports)") was not played, and a [penalty shoot-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)") was used to determine the winner (Regulations Article 2.4.3).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-6) The qualifying stages were structured as follows:

- **First stage (6 teams):** The three winners of the first stage advanced to the second stage to join the 13 teams which were given byes to the second stage.
- **Second stage (16 teams):** The eight winners of the second stage advanced to the third stage.
- **Third stage (8 teams):** The four winners of the third stage advanced to the group stage to join the 28 direct entrants. The four teams eliminated in the third stage entered the [Copa Sudamericana group stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Sudamericana_group_stage "2025 Copa Sudamericana group stage").

## Group stage

Main article: [2025 Copa Libertadores group stage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores_group_stage "2025 Copa Libertadores group stage")

In the group stage, each group was played on a home-and-away [round-robin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round-robin_tournament "Round-robin tournament") basis. Teams were ranked according to the following criteria: 1. [Points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Points_(association_football) "Points (association football)") (3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw, and 0 points for a loss); 2. [Goal difference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goal_difference "Goal difference"); 3. Goals scored; 4. Away goals scored; 5. CONMEBOL ranking (Regulations Article 2.4.2).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-6)

The winners and runners-up of each group advanced to the [round of 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores_final_stages#Round_of_16 "2025 Copa Libertadores final stages") of the [final stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores_final_stages "2025 Copa Libertadores final stages"). The third-placed teams of each group entered the [knockout round play-offs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Sudamericana_final_stages#Knockout_round_play-offs "2025 Copa Sudamericana final stages") of the [2025 Copa Sudamericana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Sudamericana "2025 Copa Sudamericana").

## Final stages

Main article: [2025 Copa Libertadores final stages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores_final_stages "2025 Copa Libertadores final stages")

Starting from the round of 16, the teams played a [single-elimination tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-elimination_tournament "Single-elimination tournament") with the following rules:[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Copa_Libertadores#cite_note-regulations-6)

- In the round of 16, quarter-finals and semi-finals, each tie was played on a home-and-away [two-legged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-legged_tie "Two-legged tie") basis, with the higher-seeded team hosting the second leg (Regulations Article 2.2.3.2). If tied on aggregate, [extra time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtime_(sports)#Association_football "Overtime (sports)") was not played, and a [penalty shoot-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)") was used to determine the winners (Regulations Article 2.4.3).
- The final was played as a single match at a venue pre-selected by CONMEBOL, with the higher-seeded team designated as the "home" team for administrative purposes (Regulations Article 2.2.3.5). If tied after regulation, 30 minutes of extra time were played. If still tied after extra time, a penalty shoot-out was used to determine the winners (Regulations Article 2.4.4).

# Libertadores 2025 Draw: Groups, Fixtures & Key Matchups

The CONMEBOL Libertadores 2025 group stage draw took place on Monday, March 17, 2025, in Luque, Paraguay, setting the stage for South America’s premier club football tournament.

The draw has created several intriguing groups, with defending champions Botafogo and other Brazilian powerhouses learning their fate in the competition’s first phase.

Defending champion Botafogo headlines Group A, where they will face Argentina’s Estudiantes, Universidad de Chile, and Venezuela’s Carabobo FC. This group presents a balanced challenge for the Brazilian side looking to secure back-to-back titles after their dramatic 2024 triumph over Atlético Mineiro.

Flamengo, one of Brazil’s most popular clubs, was drawn into Group C alongside Ecuador’s LDU Quito, Venezuela’s Deportivo Táchira, and Argentina’s Central Córdoba. With their impressive roster and passionate fan base, Flamengo enters as favorites in this group.

São Paulo finds itself in Group D with Paraguay’s Libertad, Argentina’s Talleres, and Peru’s Alianza Lima. This group is particularly notable as Alianza Lima secured their spot after eliminating Boca Juniors in a dramatic penalty shootout during the qualifying rounds.

![CONMEBOL Libertadores 2025 Group Stage Draw Unveils Exciting Matchups](https://www.riotimesonline.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Y4Eoo1dsCHytUy3S0-300x169.webp)CONMEBOL Libertadores 2025 Group Stage Draw Unveils Exciting Matchups.

Group E features Fortaleza alongside Copa Sudamericana champions Racing (Argentina), Chilean powerhouse [Colo-Colo](https://www.colocolo.cl/), and Colombia’s Atlético Bucaramanga. This represents one of the most competitive groups in the tournament, with Racing entering as a particularly dangerous opponent.

Perhaps the most intriguing draw is Group F, which pits two Brazilian clubs—Internacional and Bahia—against each other, alongside Uruguay’s Nacional and Colombia’s Atlético Nacional.
